title: Gardens in the Sky
paras: In many large cities, space at ground level is expensive and limited. As a result, architects and city planners have started to look upwards. Rooftop gardens, which were once seen as a luxury for wealthy homeowners, are now appearing on schools, hospitals, office blocks and even bus shelters.

The benefits of these gardens are both environmental and social. Plants on roofs absorb rainwater, which reduces the pressure on city drainage systems during heavy storms. They also help to cool buildings in summer. A study in Toronto found that a green roof could lower the temperature of the roof surface by more than 20 degrees Celsius on a hot day, which means that less energy is needed for air conditioning.

Rooftop gardens can also improve the quality of city life. Office workers who have access to a garden during their breaks report lower levels of stress, and some companies use their roofs to grow vegetables for staff canteens. In Singapore, a number of public housing blocks have community gardens on top, where residents of different ages meet and share their harvest.

However, building a garden on a roof is not simple. The structure must be strong enough to carry the weight of wet soil, which can be very heavy. Older buildings often need expensive strengthening work before a garden can be added. In addition, a waterproof layer has to be installed to stop water from leaking into the rooms below, and the plants must be chosen carefully because roofs are usually windier and drier than gardens on the ground.

Despite these challenges, several cities now encourage green roofs. Since 2009, Toronto has required many new large buildings to include one, and some European cities offer money to property owners who install them. Supporters believe that, in the future, the view from a city tower may be more green than grey.

title: Sleep and the Learning Brain
paras: For centuries, sleep was regarded as a passive state in which the body simply rested. Today, however, researchers see it as an active and highly organised process that is essential for learning. Experiments in sleep laboratories have shown that the brain does not switch off at night; instead, it replays and reorganises the information it has collected during the day.

One of the clearest demonstrations came from studies with rats. Scientists recorded the activity of nerve cells in the hippocampus, a region of the brain linked to memory, while the animals learned to find their way through a maze. When the rats later fell asleep, the same cells fired again in almost the same order, as if the animals were mentally running through the maze. Rats that were woken up during this replay performed worse the next day.

Human studies point in the same direction. In a typical experiment, volunteers learn a list of word pairs or a sequence of finger movements in the evening. Half of them then sleep normally, while the other half stay awake. When both groups are tested twelve hours later, those who have slept usually remember significantly more. Interestingly, sleep seems to help most with material that has been only partly learned, rather than with information that is already well known.

Different stages of sleep appear to have different functions. Deep, slow-wave sleep, which dominates the first half of the night, is thought to strengthen memories of facts and events. Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, which becomes longer towards morning, may be more important for emotional memories and for creative problem-solving. Cutting sleep short by getting up very early may therefore remove a disproportionate amount of REM sleep.

These findings have practical implications for students. Staying up all night before an examination is likely to be counter-productive, because new information has little chance to be consolidated. Several researchers recommend reviewing difficult material shortly before going to bed and then revising it again the following day. Even a short daytime nap of around sixty to ninety minutes has been shown to improve performance on some memory tasks.

title: Turning the Sea into Drinking Water
paras: Although nearly three-quarters of the Earth's surface is covered by water, less than one per cent of it is fresh water that is readily accessible for human use. With populations growing and rainfall patterns becoming less predictable, a number of countries have turned to desalination – the removal of salt from seawater – as a means of securing their supplies. More than 20,000 desalination plants are now in operation worldwide, and the Middle East alone accounts for nearly half of global capacity.

The earliest large-scale plants relied on thermal methods, in which seawater is heated until it evaporates, leaving the salt behind; the vapour is then condensed into fresh water. Such plants consume vast quantities of energy and were viable mainly in places where fuel was cheap. Since the 1980s, however, they have been steadily overtaken by reverse osmosis, a process in which seawater is forced at high pressure through membranes whose pores are small enough to block salt molecules. Advances in membrane design and the introduction of devices that recover energy from the high-pressure waste stream have cut the electricity needed per cubic metre by more than half.

Even so, desalination remains considerably more expensive than treating river or ground water, and its environmental costs are a matter of growing concern. For every litre of fresh water produced, a plant typically generates around one and a half litres of brine – a concentrated salt solution that often contains traces of chemicals used to clean the membranes. When this is discharged back into the sea, it tends to sink and spread across the seabed, where it can harm organisms that cannot tolerate high salinity. Intake pipes pose a further problem, since fish larvae and plankton may be drawn in with the seawater.

Engineers are exploring several ways to reduce this impact. Diffusers can be fitted to outlet pipes so that brine is mixed rapidly with surrounding water, and some plants dilute their discharge with treated wastewater before releasing it. A more ambitious idea is to treat brine as a resource rather than as waste. Pilot projects have extracted magnesium, lithium and other valuable minerals from it, although none has yet proved commercially viable on a large scale.

Critics argue that, for many regions, money spent on desalination would be better invested in repairing leaking pipes, recycling wastewater and encouraging more efficient irrigation, which can save water far more cheaply. Supporters reply that these measures, while valuable, cannot on their own meet the demands of rapidly expanding coastal cities. What seems clear is that desalination will be one tool among many, and that its future depends heavily on whether it can be powered by renewable energy.

title: The Politics of the Map
paras: To most people, a map is a neutral record of the world: a scaled-down, objective picture of coastlines, rivers and roads. Historians of cartography, however, have increasingly insisted that every map is an argument. Choices about what to include, what to omit, where to place the centre and how to represent a curved surface on a flat sheet inevitably reflect the priorities – and sometimes the prejudices – of the people who made it.

The problem of projection illustrates the point. Because a sphere cannot be flattened without distortion, cartographers must decide which properties to preserve. Gerardus Mercator's projection of 1569 kept angles accurate, which made it invaluable to navigators plotting straight-line compass courses. The price was a dramatic exaggeration of areas far from the equator: Greenland appears roughly the size of Africa, although Africa is in fact about fourteen times larger. For centuries, this navigational tool also served as the standard image of the world in schoolrooms, and some critics have argued that it subtly enlarged the apparent importance of Europe and North America.

In 1973 the German historian Arno Peters launched a fierce public campaign for an "equal-area" projection, which he presented as a fairer alternative. His map was adopted by several aid agencies and churches, yet professional cartographers were largely unimpressed. They pointed out that equal-area projections had been described more than a century earlier, and that Peters' version badly distorted shapes, stretching tropical continents into elongated forms. The controversy revealed less about mathematics than about the symbolic weight that people attach to maps.

Maps have also been used more directly as instruments of power. During the colonial era, surveys allowed governments to tax land, settle disputes and plan the extraction of resources, while the act of naming places on paper often erased the names used by indigenous inhabitants. Borders drawn with a ruler across territories that their designers had never visited continue to shape political conflicts today. Conversely, communities have in recent decades produced "counter-maps" documenting traditional land use, and such maps have occasionally been accepted as evidence in courts.

Digital mapping has not ended these debates; it has given them new forms. Online map services can display different borders depending on the country from which they are viewed, and the decision about which businesses appear at a given zoom level has commercial consequences. Moreover, because these maps are generated by algorithms trained on existing data, areas that are poorly documented – often poorer neighbourhoods or rural regions – can remain all but invisible. The map, it seems, is still an argument; the difference is that its authors are harder to identify.

title: How Honeybees Communicate
paras: Honeybees live in large colonies that may contain tens of thousands of individuals. To survive, a colony must collect enormous amounts of nectar and pollen from flowers that are often scattered over a wide area. Searching blindly would waste time and energy, so bees have developed a remarkable way of sharing information about where food can be found.

When a forager bee discovers a rich source of food, it returns to the hive and performs a series of movements known as the "waggle dance." The bee runs in a straight line while shaking its body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the run. ■ The angle of the straight run in relation to the vertical surface of the honeycomb indicates the direction of the food relative to the position of the sun. ■ The length of the waggle run tells the other bees how far away the food is: the longer the run, the greater the distance. ■ Other bees follow the dancer closely, touching it with their antennae, and then fly out to find the flowers themselves. ■

The meaning of the dance was first explained by the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who studied bees for decades and received a Nobel Prize in 1973. At first, many scientists doubted that insects could communicate in such an abstract way. Later experiments, including some using small robotic bees that performed the dance, confirmed that the movements really do guide other foragers.

Scent also plays an important role. Bees that follow a dance can smell the flowers the dancer has visited, which helps them recognize the right flowers when they arrive. In this way, movement and smell work together to make the colony an efficient food-gathering team.

title: What Causes Ice Ages?
paras: During the last two and a half million years, the Earth has repeatedly alternated between long glacial periods, when vast ice sheets covered much of North America and northern Europe, and shorter, warmer interglacial periods like the one we live in today. For much of the nineteenth century, scientists struggled to explain why these dramatic shifts should occur at all.

The most influential explanation was developed in the early twentieth century by the Serbian mathematician Milutin Milanković. He proposed that ice ages are paced by slow, regular changes in the Earth's orbit and orientation. ■ The shape of the orbit varies from nearly circular to slightly elliptical over a cycle of about 100,000 years. ■ The tilt of the Earth's axis shifts between roughly 22 and 24.5 degrees over 41,000 years, and the axis also wobbles like a spinning top over a period of around 23,000 years. ■ Together, these cycles alter the amount of sunlight reaching high northern latitudes in summer. ■

Milanković reasoned that the key factor was not winter cold but summer warmth. If northern summers are cool enough, some of the previous winter's snow survives until the next winter. Year after year, the snow accumulates and is compressed into ice, and because ice reflects most of the sunlight that strikes it, the growing ice sheets cool the planet still further. This process, in which an initial change is amplified, is called a positive feedback.

For decades the theory remained controversial, partly because there was no reliable way to date past climate changes. The breakthrough came in the 1970s, when scientists analysed cores of sediment drilled from the ocean floor. The chemical composition of tiny fossil shells in these cores revealed past temperatures and ice volumes, and the results showed cycles matching Milanković's predictions remarkably well.

Nevertheless, orbital changes alone cannot account for the full size of the temperature swings. Air bubbles trapped in Antarctic ice show that the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere rose and fell along with the ice ages, strengthening the effect of the orbital cycles. Scientists today therefore regard orbital variations as the "pacemaker" of ice ages, while feedbacks involving ice, oceans and greenhouse gases determine how large the changes become.

title: The Printing Press and the Spread of Knowledge
paras: Before the middle of the fifteenth century, books in Europe were produced almost entirely by hand. Professional scribes, many of them working in monasteries, could spend months copying a single volume, and the resulting manuscripts were so costly that only churches, universities and the wealthiest individuals could afford substantial collections. Errors crept in with every copy, so that two versions of the same text frequently disagreed.

Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith from the German city of Mainz, combined several existing technologies into a system that transformed this situation. His crucial innovation was a hand mould for casting large numbers of identical metal letters, or "type," which could be arranged into pages, inked, printed and then rearranged for the next job. ■ He also developed an oil-based ink that adhered well to metal and adapted the screw press, a device already used for pressing grapes and olives. ■ Gutenberg's famous Bible, completed around 1455, demonstrated that printed books could match the beauty of the finest manuscripts. ■ Ironically, Gutenberg himself profited little; a lawsuit cost him much of his equipment. ■

The new technology spread with astonishing speed. By 1500, printing shops had been established in more than 250 European towns, and it has been estimated that some twenty million volumes had already been produced. Prices fell sharply, and books became accessible to merchants, lawyers and craftsmen who would never have owned a manuscript. Printers, who needed to sell their products, quickly diversified beyond religious texts into grammars, almanacs, medical handbooks and pamphlets on current affairs.

Historians continue to debate the consequences. Some argue that printing was a precondition for the Protestant Reformation, since Martin Luther's writings circulated in hundreds of thousands of copies within a few years. Others emphasize its role in the Scientific Revolution: because printed tables, diagrams and observations could be reproduced exactly, scholars in different countries could build on one another's work rather than wasting effort correcting copying errors. Standardized printed texts also encouraged the stabilization of spelling and grammar in vernacular languages.

Yet the transformation was neither immediate nor complete. Literacy rates remained low for centuries in many regions, and handwritten copies continued to circulate, particularly for texts that authorities wished to restrict. Moreover, the flood of printed material included much that was inaccurate or deliberately misleading, prompting complaints that readers were being overwhelmed – a concern that sounds strikingly familiar in the digital age.

title: Partnership and Crisis on Coral Reefs
title_fa: همزیستی و بحران در صخره‌های مرجانی
paras: Coral reefs occupy less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they support roughly a quarter of all known marine species. This productivity is paradoxical, because the clear tropical waters in which reefs flourish are notoriously poor in nutrients. The solution to the paradox lies in an intimate partnership between corals and microscopic algae called zooxanthellae, which live inside the tissues of the coral animals themselves.

Each coral polyp is a small, soft-bodied animal related to jellyfish. The algae within its cells carry out photosynthesis, supplying the polyp with sugars and other organic compounds that may meet up to ninety per cent of its energy needs. ■ In return, the coral provides the algae with a protected environment and with the carbon dioxide and nitrogen-rich wastes that they require. ■ Nutrients are thus recycled with extraordinary efficiency between partner and host, rather than being lost to the surrounding water. ■ The energy surplus allows corals to deposit calcium carbonate skeletons at a rate sufficient to build structures that, over thousands of years, may stretch for hundreds of kilometres. ■

The partnership, however, operates within narrow limits. When water temperatures rise just one or two degrees Celsius above the usual summer maximum for several weeks, the algae's photosynthetic machinery becomes damaged and begins to produce harmful reactive oxygen compounds. The coral responds by expelling the algae, and because the algae supply most of the coral's colour, the animal's white skeleton becomes visible through its transparent tissue – a phenomenon known as bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead, but it is starving; if favourable conditions do not return within a few weeks, it is likely to perish.

Mass bleaching events, once virtually unknown, have become increasingly frequent as ocean temperatures have risen. The Great Barrier Reef experienced severe episodes in 1998, 2002, 2016, 2017 and 2020, and recovery between events has been incomplete. Some researchers had hoped that corals would adapt by acquiring more heat-tolerant strains of algae. There is evidence that such shifts occur, but they appear to be too slow, and the tolerant strains sometimes supply less food, leaving the coral weaker.

Scientists are now pursuing interventions that would have seemed fanciful a generation ago, from breeding corals selectively for heat resistance to shading reefs with fine sprays of seawater droplets. Most specialists stress, nevertheless, that such measures can at best buy time. Without substantial reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, they warn, the conditions to which the coral-algae partnership has been adapted for millions of years will simply cease to exist in many parts of the tropics.

title: Urban Heat Islands
paras: Cities are often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island. The usual explanation emphasizes materials: asphalt and concrete absorb sunlight during the day and release the stored heat slowly at night. Yet materials are only part of the story. The geometry of streets also matters, since tall buildings lining narrow streets trap radiation that would otherwise escape to the sky. Furthermore, the scarcity of vegetation deprives cities of the cooling that plants provide when water evaporates from their leaves.

Because the effect is strongest at night, its consequences are frequently underestimated. During heat waves, the absence of nighttime relief can be more dangerous to health than high daytime temperatures, particularly for elderly residents who lack air conditioning.

title: Oral History and Its Critics
paras: When oral history emerged as an academic practice in the mid-twentieth century, many historians regarded it with suspicion. Memories, they argued, are notoriously unreliable: people forget, embellish, and unconsciously reshape their recollections to fit later beliefs. Documents, by contrast, were assumed to record events as they happened. Proponents of oral history responded in two ways. First, they pointed out that documents are hardly free of distortion, since they are produced by individuals with their own interests and are preserved selectively by institutions. Second, and more provocatively, they insisted that the so-called unreliability of memory is itself a source of historical insight.

If a factory worker recalls a strike as a moment of triumph although it ended in defeat, the discrepancy reveals how the event was understood and what it came to mean in the community. On this view, the task of the oral historian is not merely to extract facts from testimony but to interpret the significance that people attach to the past. Critics have objected that such an approach risks blurring the line between history and literature; supporters reply that the line was never as sharp as traditional historians supposed.

title: The Island Rule
paras: Biologists have long observed that animals isolated on islands tend to evolve toward unusual body sizes: large mammals such as elephants and deer often become dwarfed, while small animals such as rodents sometimes become giants. This pattern, termed the island rule, has typically been attributed to ecological release. On islands, predators are frequently absent, and resources are limited; large species, freed from the need to be big for defense and constrained by scarce food, shrink, whereas small species, freed from the need to hide and from competition with larger rivals, grow.

Recent analyses, however, have complicated this tidy account. A survey of hundreds of island populations found that the rule holds strongly for some groups, such as carnivores and certain rodents, but weakly or not at all for others, including many bats and birds. Moreover, the magnitude of change correlates with island area and isolation in ways that the simple model does not predict. Some researchers now suggest that the island rule is not a single phenomenon at all but a statistical tendency produced by several distinct processes, each operating more strongly in some lineages than in others. Far from diminishing the rule's interest, this reinterpretation arguably makes islands even more valuable as natural laboratories, since the variations themselves can be used to test which mechanisms matter where.

title: Markets and Moral Motivation
paras: Standard economic theory treats incentives as additive: if people are already inclined to perform a socially valuable act, offering them money to do so should, at worst, leave their behavior unchanged and, at best, increase it. A growing body of evidence suggests that this assumption is sometimes false. In a widely cited study of Israeli day-care centers, the introduction of a modest fine for parents who arrived late to collect their children was followed not by a decline but by a marked increase in late arrivals; more striking still, when the fine was abolished, lateness remained at its new, higher level.

The researchers interpreted the result as a case of "crowding out." Before the fine, parents had understood punctuality as an obligation toward the teachers, enforced by guilt; the fine reframed lateness as a service that could be purchased, and once the moral framing had been displaced, removing the price did not restore it. Skeptics have cautioned against generalizing from such cases, noting that in many contexts monetary incentives work much as theory predicts and that the size of the payment matters: small sums may insult, whereas large ones persuade. The more defensible conclusion, then, is not that markets inevitably corrode morality, but that the meaning participants attach to a transaction is itself an economic variable – one that conventional models, by treating preferences as fixed, are poorly equipped to capture.

title: Microplastics in Our Water
paras: Microplastics are pieces of plastic smaller than five millimetres. Some are made deliberately, such as the tiny beads once added to face scrubs, but most come from larger items that slowly break apart in sunlight and seawater. Washing synthetic clothes also releases thousands of plastic fibres, which pass through treatment plants and enter rivers.

Scientists have now found microplastics almost everywhere they have looked, from Arctic ice to bottled drinking water. Their effects on human health are still unclear. However, researchers are concerned because the particles can carry harmful chemicals and are easily swallowed by fish and other animals. Several countries have already banned plastic microbeads in cosmetics, and some washing-machine makers are developing filters to catch fibres before they leave the home.

title: The Remote Work Revolution
paras: Before 2020, working from home was a privilege enjoyed by a small minority of employees. The pandemic changed that almost overnight, as offices closed and companies discovered that many tasks could be performed perfectly well from a kitchen table. Several years later, a large proportion of office workers in developed economies continue to spend at least part of the week at home.

Supporters of remote work point to the time and money saved on commuting, as well as greater flexibility for parents and carers. Some studies have also found modest gains in productivity, particularly for tasks that require concentration. Critics, however, argue that remote arrangements weaken the informal contacts through which junior staff learn and through which new ideas often emerge. Managers also report difficulties in building trust within teams whose members rarely meet.

As a result, many organisations have settled on hybrid models, in which employees come to the office on certain days. The challenge now is to make those days worthwhile, using them for collaboration and mentoring rather than for tasks that could be done equally well at home.

title: The Puzzle of the Placebo
paras: A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill, that is given to patients in clinical trials so that the effects of a real drug can be measured against it. For decades, the improvement that many patients experience after taking a placebo was regarded as a nuisance – a source of "noise" that researchers needed to subtract. Increasingly, however, scientists are treating the placebo effect as a genuine phenomenon worth studying in its own right.

Brain-imaging studies have shown that, in people who expect pain relief, placebos can trigger the release of the body's own pain-relieving chemicals. The effect depends heavily on context: larger pills tend to work better than small ones, injections better than tablets, and expensive "brands" better than cheap ones. Remarkably, some trials have found that placebos can help even when patients are told openly that they are receiving an inactive pill, which challenges the assumption that deception is essential.

The placebo effect has limits. It can reduce symptoms such as pain, nausea and fatigue, but it does not shrink tumours or cure infections. Nevertheless, a better understanding of how expectations shape experience may help doctors communicate in ways that strengthen the benefits of real treatments.

title: When Languages Disappear
paras: Of the roughly 7,000 languages spoken in the world today, linguists estimate that as many as half may cease to be spoken by the end of this century. Language death is not new – countless languages have vanished throughout history – but its current pace is unprecedented. Most endangered languages have few speakers, many of whom are elderly, and children are no longer acquiring them at home.

The causes are rarely linguistic. Communities shift to dominant languages because those languages offer access to education, employment and political participation; in some cases, earlier generations were actively punished for speaking their ancestral tongue at school. The loss is not merely sentimental. Each language encodes a distinctive way of categorising experience, and many contain detailed knowledge of local plants, animals and ecosystems that has never been written down.

Revitalisation efforts have had mixed results. Hebrew, revived as an everyday spoken language in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries, is often cited as a success, while Welsh and Māori have regained ground through immersion schooling and broadcasting. Yet such cases depend on sustained institutional support and, above all, on the willingness of parents to speak the language to their children. Digital tools – from recorded dictionaries to social-media groups – can assist, but they cannot substitute for a community of everyday users.

title: Is It Time for a Digital Detox?
paras: The average adult now checks their phone dozens of times a day, often without any clear purpose. For some people, this constant connection has begun to feel less like a convenience and more like a burden. As a result, the idea of a "digital detox" – a period of time without smartphones, social media or other devices – has become increasingly popular.

Advocates claim that even a short break can improve sleep, concentration and mood. Some hotels now offer packages in which guests hand in their phones at reception, and summer camps for adults promise a return to conversation and outdoor activity. Research on the subject, however, is mixed. While several studies have found that reducing social-media use can lower feelings of loneliness and anxiety, others suggest that the benefits of a complete break may disappear soon after people reconnect.

Many psychologists therefore recommend changing habits rather than escaping technology altogether. Simple steps include turning off non-essential notifications, keeping phones out of the bedroom and setting specific times for checking messages. The goal, they argue, is not to reject useful tools, but to make sure that we use them deliberately instead of reacting automatically every time a screen lights up.

title: The Four-Day Week: Utopia or Experiment?
title_fa: هفتهٔ کاری چهارروزه: آرمان‌شهر یا آزمایش؟
paras: A century ago, the eight-hour day and the two-day weekend were regarded by many employers as dangerously utopian demands. Today they are taken for granted, and a growing movement argues that the next step should be a four-day working week with no loss of pay. Proponents insist that this is not a call for people to do less, but for organisations to stop confusing hours spent at a desk with value produced.

Large trials conducted in several countries have provided encouraging, if not conclusive, evidence. In a widely reported British pilot involving around sixty companies, most participants chose to keep the shorter week after the trial ended, citing lower staff turnover, fewer sick days and broadly stable revenue. Employees, unsurprisingly, reported less burnout and more time for family and exercise. Sceptics, however, point out that the firms involved volunteered to take part and were therefore likely to be those best suited to the change.

Indeed, the model translates unevenly across sectors. Software developers or marketing teams may be able to eliminate unnecessary meetings and compress their work, but a hospital, a school or a bus company cannot simply close for an extra day; it must hire additional staff, which raises costs. There is also a risk that compressing five days of work into four simply intensifies pressure, replacing one form of exhaustion with another.

Perhaps the most valuable outcome of the debate is that it has forced managers to scrutinise how time is actually used. Even organisations that never adopt a four-day week may benefit from asking which meetings, reports and rituals genuinely contribute to their goals – and which survive merely out of habit.
